Using the new ligand–receptor pairs, they highlight co-expression of excitatory and inhibitory channels in single hermaphrodite neurons and propose a connectome synaptic-polarity model.
summaries.advanced: LGC-39 as a “truly polymodal” channel is the authors’ first-evidence claim. The polarity model is predictive, not a full physiological census of every synapse. The abstract does not give expression counts or electrophysiological EC50 values. Catalog dataset tag DS01 reflects use of the C. elegans connectome for polarity mapping.

plain_language_summary: Brain chemicals can open gates that either excite or quiet a cell. In the worm, this team finds new quieting gates that prefer choline, one gate that responds to more than one chemical, and many cells that carry both “go” and “stop” gates.

ocar.opportunity: Choosing left versus right is often treated as a high-level cognitive problem, yet urgent defensive escapes need immediate, local implementation of trajectory direction.
ocar.challenge: The spinal circuit that amplifies brainstem escape commands and enforces directionality in adult zebrafish was unknown.
ocar.action: Guan, Xu, Song, El Manira, and colleagues combine electrophysiology, serial block-face electron microscopy, and behavior to reconstruct a specialized spinal circuit, including cholinergic V2a interneurons expressing Chx10.
ocar.resolution: Segmentally repeating cholinergic V2a cells act as a hub that receives and amplifies escape commands and, via fast axo-axonic synapses, drives all fast motor neurons and commissural interneurons to set escape direction. Unilateral ablation of these V2a cells eliminated escape-command propagation.
ocar.future_work: The work shows that local spinal circuits can implement directionality of urgent survival actions in vertebrates.

summaries.beginner: When a fish must dart away, it cannot wait for a slow decision about left or right. This study finds a repeating spinal circuit that boosts the brain’s escape shout and aims the body through fast, axon-to-axon contacts.
summaries.intermediate: In PNAS (2021), Guan et al. map a specialized adult zebrafish spinal circuit for escape direction using electrophysiology, SBF-SEM, and behavior. Cholinergic V2a interneurons expressing Chx10 form a segmentally repeating hub that amplifies brainstem escape commands and delivers excitation via axo-axonic synapses to fast motor neurons and commissural interneurons. Unilateral ablation of these V2a cells abolished command propagation.
summaries.advanced: The “full functional connectome” claim is for this specialized escape circuit, not the entire spinal cord. Ablation eliminating propagation is a strong causal result as stated, but the abstract does not report sample sizes. Axo-axonic transmission bypassing soma and dendrites is a key anatomical motif; generalization to other vertebrates is argued by homology of V2a/Chx10, not shown here. Catalog tags include DS15 zebrafish and SBF-SEM.

plain_language_summary: When a fish must dart away, it cannot wait for a slow decision about left or right. This study finds a repeating spinal circuit that boosts the brain’s escape shout and aims the body through fast, axon-to-axon contacts.

ocar.opportunity: Individual neurons are sophisticated, but brain computation arises from synaptic patterns that form specialized circuits, from microcircuit motifs to global architectures.
ocar.challenge: Molecular, anatomical, and physiological data on single neurons have exploded, yet general principles of how those neurons communicate in circuits are still scattered across scales and species.
ocar.action: Luo reviews circuit architectures using tracing, recording, perturbation, and modeling, treating microcircuit motifs as “words” and larger plans as “sentences,” and considering development and evolution.
ocar.resolution: He synthesizes feedforward excitation/inhibition, feedback and lateral inhibition, mutual inhibition, topographic maps, parallel processing, dimensionality expansion, biased neuromodulatory subsystems, and recurrent loops, plus how molecular gradients versus combinatorial surface codes build them.
ocar.future_work: He calls for circuit mapping across species, multi-scale motif operation, and integrating structure, function, development, and evolution—work that may also inspire artificial intelligence.

summaries.beginner: A brain is not just a pile of cells; it is cells wired in repeating patterns, like words built into sentences. This review gathers those patterns and asks how they arise in development and evolution.
summaries.intermediate: In Science (2021), Liqun Luo reviews neuronal circuit architectures from microcircuit motifs to larger plans. Core motifs include feedforward excitation and inhibition, feedback and lateral inhibition, and mutual inhibition; larger plans include continuous topography, discrete parallel processing, dimensionality expansion, biased neuromodulatory projections, and recurrent loops. He also discusses evolutionary conservation versus independent invention and developmental strategies that specify many connections with relatively few proteins.
summaries.advanced: This is a wide-ranging review; the abstract’s “about 100 billion neurons, each with thousands of synapses” is a human-brain scale illustration, not a new measurement. Many architectures are noted as still “awaiting discovery.” The letters/words/sentences metaphor is pedagogical, not a formal theory. Outlook items (serial EM, trans-synaptic tracing) are recommendations.

plain_language_summary: A brain is not just a pile of cells; it is cells wired in repeating patterns, like words built into sentences. This review gathers those patterns and asks how they arise in development and evolution.

ocar.opportunity: Synaptic connectomes are the anatomical foundation for nematode circuit function, but extrasynaptic volume transmission can communicate without synapses.
ocar.challenge: No experimental evidence had identified nematode body-cavity fluid as a vehicle for neuropeptide or biogenic-amine transmission, despite hints in C. elegans.
ocar.action: Atkinson, Liu, Mousley, and colleagues analyze Ascaris suum pseudocoelomic fluid (PCF), focusing on FLP-18 peptides that potently stimulate female reproductive organs despite being expressed in anatomically distant, non-synaptic cells.
ocar.resolution: As-PCF contains many neuropeptides; As-FLP-18A dominates the peptidome; PCF potently modulates reproductive muscle ex vivo like synthetic FLP-18, activates C. elegans FLP-18 receptors NPR-4 and NPR-5, and alters C. elegans behavior. FLP-18 and its receptors show pan-phylum nematode distribution.
ocar.future_work: They argue extrasynaptic volume routes belong in the functional nematode connectome, with implications for receptor deorphanization and anthelmintic discovery.

summaries.beginner: Wiring maps show contacts between worm nerve cells, but messages can also travel in body fluid. This study finds peptide messages in a parasitic worm’s body fluid that can still change muscle and behavior without a direct nerve contact.
summaries.intermediate: In ACS Chemical Neuroscience (2021), Atkinson et al. provide experimental evidence for extrasynaptic neuropeptide transmission via Ascaris suum pseudocoelomic fluid. As-PCF contains FMRFamide-like peptides and neuropeptide-like proteins, dominated by As-FLP-18A; it modulates reproductive muscle like synthetic FLP-18, activates C. elegans NPR-4 and NPR-5, and changes C. elegans behavior. FLP-18 signaling components appear across nematodes.
summaries.advanced: This is the “first direct experimental evidence” claim for a PCF peptide route, not a disproof of synaptic FLP-18 roles. Dominance of As-FLP-18A is a peptidome statement without quantitative abundances in the abstract. Behavioral effects in C. elegans from A. suum PCF show cross-species receptor engagement; native C. elegans PCF transmission is inferred. Catalog DS01 tag reflects C. elegans receptor/behavior assays.

plain_language_summary: Wiring maps show contacts between worm nerve cells, but messages can also travel in body fluid. This study finds peptide messages in a parasitic worm’s body fluid that can still change muscle and behavior without a direct nerve contact.

ocar.opportunity: Direction selectivity is a classic neural computation; in non-primate mammals it arises in starburst amacrine dendrites that inhibit ON and ON-OFF direction-selective ganglion cells.
ocar.challenge: Primates have starburst amacrine cells, but their connectivity is unknown and whether primate direction-selective ganglion cells exist remains open, with direction selectivity classically placed in visual cortex.
ocar.action: Patterson, Bembry, Mazzeferri, Neitz, Rieke, Soetedjo, and Neitz reconstruct the primate ON starburst circuit from a serial EM volume of macaque central retina.
ocar.resolution: The structural basis for computing and conferring directional selectivity is conserved, and starbursts selectively target a single ganglion-cell type, a candidate homolog of mammalian ON-sustained dsRGCs that project to the accessory optic system for gaze-stabilizing reflexes.
ocar.future_work: They conclude the capacity to compute motion direction is present in primate retina, earlier than classically thought, and they outline how ancestral motion circuits are conserved.

summaries.beginner: Many mammals compute motion direction in the eye itself; primates were thought to wait until the brain. This macaque retina map suggests the same early motion machinery is present and aimed at a specific output cell type.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2021 bioRxiv preprint, Patterson et al. reconstruct the ON starburst amacrine circuit from serial EM of macaque central retina. They report conservation of the structural basis by which starbursts compute and confer direction selectivity, with selective targeting of one ganglion-cell type homologous to ON-sustained dsRGCs of the accessory optic system. The result places motion-direction computation earlier in the primate visual system than the cortical-centric textbook view.
summaries.advanced: This is a connectomic preprint; physiological direction selectivity of the candidate primate dsRGC is not demonstrated in the abstract. Homology to accessory-optic ON-sustained dsRGCs is proposed from targeting, not from projection tracing here. Catalog organism tag says “other” and dataset mouse retina—privilege the abstract’s macaque central retina. Conservation refers to structural motifs, not a full functional duplication of mouse SAC circuits.

plain_language_summary: Many mammals compute motion direction in the eye itself; primates were thought to wait until the brain. This macaque retina map suggests the same early motion machinery is present and aimed at a specific output cell type.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans produces varied motion with only 69 motor neurons and 95 muscle cells, and prior work mapped connectome roles of motor-neuron classes.
ocar.challenge: Those models had not analyzed the distribution of synaptic and gap-junction weights or shown that a motor–muscle network can oscillate for both forward and backward locomotion and switch on command.
ocar.action: Sakamoto, Soh, Suzuki, Iino, and Tsuji build a connectome-based network of A, B, D, and AS motor neurons plus muscle, with synaptic and gap connections, and train weights by backpropagation through time on command-neuron inputs and muscle activations.
ocar.resolution: The circuit generates oscillations with different phase patterns for forward versus backward movement and can switch at arbitrary times given binary command-like inputs. Trained weights follow a Boltzmann-type distribution. The model can be trained to reproduce activity patterns measured in HRB4 animals.
ocar.future_work: They suggest supervised learning of this kind may allow further analysis of complex movement-related activity patterns.

summaries.beginner: A worm crawls forward or backward using a small set of motor cells and muscles. This computer model of those cells can make both walking rhythms and switch between them when a simple command is flipped.
summaries.intermediate: In Scientific Reports (2021), Sakamoto et al. simulate a C. elegans motor-neuron and muscle network (classes A, B, D, AS) including synapses and gap junctions. Backpropagation through time, trained on command-neuron input and muscle activation, yields forward and backward oscillatory phase patterns switchable at arbitrary times. Trained synaptic and gap weights follow a Boltzmann-type distribution, and the model can reproduce HRB4 strain activity patterns.
summaries.advanced: Weight distributions are properties of the trained model, not measured biological weights. “69 motor neurons and 95 muscle cells” are background counts from the literature as cited in the abstract. Arbitrary-time switching uses binary inputs simulating command neurons, not recorded command-cell spike trains. HRB4 reproduction shows the framework can fit real activity, not that the learned weights are unique.

plain_language_summary: A worm crawls forward or backward using a small set of motor cells and muscles. This computer model of those cells can make both walking rhythms and switch between them when a simple command is flipped.

ocar.opportunity: Retinal prostheses stimulate surviving cells after degenerative disease, but restored vision quality is limited, and early plasticity may precede photoreceptor loss.
ocar.challenge: How current flows from rods to rod bipolar cells in healthy versus early-degenerated retina is not known in enough detail to improve stimulation.
ocar.action: Kosta, Iseri, Loizos, Paknahad, Pfeiffer, Sigulinsky, Anderson, Jones, and Lazzi build conductance-based Neuron models of morphologically accurate cells and synapses from serial-section TEM connectomes of healthy (RC1) and early-stage degenerated (RPC1) rabbit retina (70 nm slices).
ocar.resolution: In response to rod photocurrent, simulated rod-bipolar membrane potential in early degenerate tissue is approximately 10–20 mV lower than in wild type, primarily from reduced rod input rather than the early morphological changes. Frequency and step responses of individual rod bipolar cells do not differ significantly before substantial photoreceptor loss.
ocar.future_work: They argue such models are essential to understand current flow as degeneration progresses and to improve retinal prostheses.

summaries.beginner: When the eye’s light sensors start to fail, doctors hope to stimulate the remaining cells, but the electrical paths have already changed. This study builds computer models from detailed rabbit-retina maps and finds the remaining middle-layer cells sit at a lower voltage mainly because they get less input from rods.
summaries.intermediate: In Experimental Eye Research (2021), Kosta et al. compare current flow from rods to rod bipolar cells using TEM-based connectome models of healthy RC1 and early-degenerate RPC1 rabbit retina. Simulated rod-bipolar membrane potential is about 10–20 mV lower in early degeneration, attributed primarily to reduced rod input despite early morphological change. Individual cell frequency and step responses are reported not to differ significantly before substantial photoreceptor loss.
summaries.advanced: The 10–20 mV difference is a simulation result under photocurrent input, not an in vivo intracellular measurement reported here. “Do not differ significantly” for frequency/step responses lacks p-values and n in the abstract. Early RPC1 morphology is altered but is not the main cause of the voltage shift in the authors’ account. Catalog tags list mouse retina; the abstract specifies rabbit RC1/RPC1—follow the abstract.

plain_language_summary: When the eye’s light sensors start to fail, doctors hope to stimulate the remaining cells, but the electrical paths have already changed. This study builds computer models from detailed rabbit-retina maps and finds the remaining middle-layer cells sit at a lower voltage mainly because they get less input from rods.

ocar.opportunity: From mouse to primate there is a discontinuity in motion-direction coding: non-primate retinas have direction-selective cells and circuits, whereas primate direction selectivity is a hallmark of visual cortex and had not been found in retina despite significant effort.
ocar.challenge: Whether primate retina contains direction-selective cell types and the synaptic motifs that create them remained open.
ocar.action: Kim, Peterson, Crook, Dacey, and colleagues combine light-evoked recordings with connectomic reconstruction in macaque retina.
ocar.resolution: They identify diverse direction-selective types, including an ON-OFF ganglion cell, a spiking ON-OFF polyaxonal amacrine, and the starburst amacrine, all direction selective. Macaque starbursts have a strong non-GABAergic antagonistic surround from excitatory bipolar input that is critical for radial motion sensitivity.
ocar.future_work: The findings open investigation of precortical primate motion circuitry.

summaries.beginner: Textbooks placed primate motion sensing mainly in visual cortex, not in the eye. This macaque study finds direction-tuned cells already in the retina and explains a special surround that helps starburst cells sense outward motion.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Communications (2021), Kim et al. combine physiology and connectomics to identify direction-selective cell types in macaque retina, including an ON-OFF ganglion cell, a spiking ON-OFF polyaxonal amacrine, and starburst amacrine cells. They report that macaque starbursts possess a strong, non-GABAergic antagonistic surround mediated by excitatory bipolar input, critical for radial motion sensitivity. The work establishes a retinal origin for primate direction selectivity.
summaries.advanced: “Despite significant effort” frames prior negatives; this paper claims positive identification of multiple DS types. The non-GABAergic surround is a mechanistic finding specific to macaque starbursts as described. Catalog dataset/organism tags say mouse retina/mouse; the abstract is macaque—ground in the abstract. Diversity of types is asserted without a count in the abstract.

plain_language_summary: Textbooks placed primate motion sensing mainly in visual cortex, not in the eye. This macaque study finds direction-tuned cells already in the retina and explains a special surround that helps starburst cells sense outward motion.

ocar.opportunity: Large neuroscience efforts such as connectomics attract attention by promising links from structure to mind.
ocar.challenge: Gomez-Marin argues these projects recurrently overpromise and underdeliver, especially when “horizontal” maps of one level (synapses) are sold as “vertical” mappings to function, behavior, and cognition.
ocar.action: In this eNeuro commentary he critically assesses claims versus results and the field’s metaphors.
ocar.resolution: He argues it is theoretically flawed at many levels to suggest connectomics will give us the mind of a mouse, human, or even a fly. Even if metaphors are not literal, they should be taken seriously.
ocar.future_work: The piece is a caution to keep levels of explanation distinct rather than a methods program.

summaries.beginner: Some big brain-mapping projects sound as if listing connections will explain thought. This commentary says that leap skips too many steps: a map of contacts is not the same as a map of mind.
summaries.intermediate: In eNeuro (2021), Gomez-Marin critiques grand projects such as connectomics for overpromising. He distinguishes horizontal results (synaptic maps) from vertical conclusions (function, behavior, cognition) and calls the suggestion that connectomics will yield the mind of a mouse, human, or fly theoretically flawed. He urges taking the field’s metaphors seriously even when they are not meant literally.
summaries.advanced: This is an opinion/significance essay without new data. It does not evaluate any specific reconstruction’s empirical quality. Use it pedagogically as a levels-of-explanation critique, not as evidence against particular connectomes. Catalog organism tag (mouse) is incidental to the rhetoric.

plain_language_summary: Some big brain-mapping projects sound as if listing connections will explain thought. This commentary says that leap skips too many steps: a map of contacts is not the same as a map of mind.

ocar.opportunity: Questions such as how circuits generate behavior are hard in inaccessible mammalian nervous systems; invertebrate circuits, especially Drosophila, have supplied much of what we know about circuit development.
ocar.challenge: Non-fly researchers may not see the larval locomotor network as a generic model for mammalian-relevant questions.
ocar.action: Hunter, Coulson, Zarin, and Baines review the Drosophila larval locomotor circuit, using the relatively complete connectome around identified interneuron A27h and relating it to similar mammalian circuits, then discuss critical periods and interindividual variability.
ocar.resolution: They argue the larval locomotor network is a useful “generic” model circuit for development and function, including topics such as critical periods and variability.
ocar.future_work: The review aims to recruit researchers who do not usually use the fly.

summaries.beginner: Mammalian brains are hard to take apart, so simpler walking circuits in young fruit flies are a practical classroom for how wiring builds behavior. This review shows how one well-mapped fly walking circuit can stand in for bigger brains.
summaries.intermediate: In Frontiers in Neural Circuits (2021), Hunter et al. promote the Drosophila larval locomotor network as a model circuit. They discuss the relatively complete connectome associated with identified interneuron A27h and analogies to mammalian circuits, then apply the system to critical periods of development and interindividual variability. The piece is written to be accessible to non-Drosophila neuroscientists.
summaries.advanced: This is a review/perspective, not a new connectome. A27h is used as an entry point to a “relatively complete” local connectome; completeness is relative to that identified neuron’s neighborhood. Mammalian analogies are pedagogical, not homology proofs. Catalog datasets include both C. elegans and Drosophila larva as comparative model-circuit context.

plain_language_summary: Mammalian brains are hard to take apart, so simpler walking circuits in young fruit flies are a practical classroom for how wiring builds behavior. This review shows how one well-mapped fly walking circuit can stand in for bigger brains.

ocar.opportunity: Completion of the C. elegans connectome four decades ago has long guided circuit work; new microscopy, computation, single-cell transcriptomes, and cell-specific tools now expand that foundation.
ocar.challenge: The original wiring diagram was incomplete in reported synapses, and linking molecular identity to behaving-animal circuit function needed new atlases.
ocar.action: Byrd and Jin mini-review re-examinations of the connectome, models of networks underlying behavior, and progress toward a molecular atlas with cell-specific manipulation in behaving animals.
ocar.resolution: Re-examination has uncovered previously unreported synaptic connections and generated models for neural networks underlying behaviors, while molecular atlases plus cell-specific tools enable precise investigation of individual neurons during behavior.
ocar.future_work: They discuss emerging findings on neuronal circuits in light of these resources.

summaries.beginner: The first complete animal wiring diagram, from a tiny worm, is being looked at again with better tools. This short review covers new connections that were missed, new models of behavior, and ways to turn single cells on or off while the worm acts.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2021), Byrd and Jin review recent C. elegans circuit advances. Improved microscopy and computation have added previously unreported synapses and supported network models of behavior. Combining single-cell transcriptomes with cell-specific tools now lets researchers manipulate individual neurons in behaving animals, progressing toward a molecular atlas of the nervous system.
summaries.advanced: This is a mini-review; newly reported synapses are not listed here. “Models for neural network underlying behaviors” is generic. Use as a pointer into 2021-era resources rather than as primary evidence. Catalog DS01 tag matches the organism/dataset focus.

plain_language_summary: The first complete animal wiring diagram, from a tiny worm, is being looked at again with better tools. This short review covers new connections that were missed, new models of behavior, and ways to turn single cells on or off while the worm acts.

ocar.opportunity: Structural connectivity is a critical determinant of network function, but many networks can yield similar responses and the same network can function differently by context, so required synapses are largely unknown.
ocar.challenge: Quantitative links from specified steady-state responses back to which synapses must exist are subtle in recurrent threshold-linear networks.
ocar.action: Biswas and Fitzgerald introduce a geometric framework that, when the number of specified response patterns does not exceed the number of input synapses, analytically calculates the solution space of all feedforward and recurrent connectivity matrices that can generate those responses, including a noise generalization.
ocar.resolution: The solution-space geometry can undergo topological transitions as allowed error increases. The characterization yields certainty conditions guaranteeing a nonzero synapse between neurons.
ocar.future_work: They propose applying the framework to neural activity data to make rigorous anatomical predictions from the model architecture.

summaries.beginner: Many different wirings can make a network behave the same way, so activity alone rarely proves a connection exists. This theory paper finds geometric conditions under which a response pattern does guarantee that two cells are linked.
summaries.intermediate: In Physical Review Research (2020), Biswas and Fitzgerald analyze recurrent networks of threshold-linear neurons. Assuming specified steady-state patterns do not outnumber input synapses, they calculate the space of all feedforward and recurrent weight matrices consistent with those responses from given inputs. With noise, that space can change topology as allowed error grows, and they derive certainty conditions for a nonzero synapse.
summaries.advanced: Results are analytical for threshold-linear neurons under a pattern-count assumption; they do not automatically apply to spiking or strongly nonlinear models. Topological transitions with error are a geometric observation that “could provide insight” into neuroscience and machine learning, not an empirical finding. Anatomical predictions require that real circuits approximately match the model class.

plain_language_summary: Many different wirings can make a network behave the same way, so activity alone rarely proves a connection exists. This theory paper finds geometric conditions under which a response pattern does guarantee that two cells are linked.

ocar.opportunity: Even relatively small portions of animal brains imaged by EM can require terabytes, making unsupervised discovery of unknown patterns essential alongside supervised detectors of known objects.
ocar.challenge: Supervised models find known patterns but scale poorly for mining patterns that are not known a priori.
ocar.action: Huang, Yang, Takemura, Rivlin, and Plaza learn a latent representation with unsupervised deep learning, using semantics-preserving augmentations so similar structures lie close in feature space, and they provide a visualization tool and software ecosystem (including Neuroglancer) for interactive analysis of fly EM volumes such as FAFB and hemibrain.
ocar.resolution: The representation enables query-by-example and clustering that correlates with biologically meaningful distinctions.
ocar.future_work: They argue this opens avenues for discovery in large EM datasets.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope brain pictures are so large that no one can browse them all by hand. This method learns a similarity space so that if you click an interesting pattern, the computer can show you other places that look the same.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2020 arXiv paper, Huang et al. train an unsupervised latent representation for massive EM volumes using augmentations that preserve semantic meaning. Applied to nanoscale fly EM, the features support query-by-example and clustering that correlates with biologically meaningful distinctions. They also introduce visualization/software for interactive analysis of such datasets.
summaries.advanced: “Correlates with biologically-meaningful distinctions” is not quantified in the abstract (no ARI/NMI). Query-by-example quality depends on the augmentation set defining “semantic meaning.” Catalog datasets DS04 FAFB and DS05 hemibrain plus Neuroglancer match the intended application domain; the abstract does not name those volumes explicitly.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope brain pictures are so large that no one can browse them all by hand. This method learns a similarity space so that if you click an interesting pattern, the computer can show you other places that look the same.

ocar.opportunity: Microtubules are biologically informative structures in EM volumes of neural tissue, but tracking them automatically is hard.
ocar.challenge: Prior tracking was too slow and inaccurate for large Drosophila neural volumes.
ocar.action: Eckstein, Buhmann, Cook, and Funke first detect sparse microtubule voxels, build a candidate graph of potential edges, then select tracks by a novel integer linear program encoding biological priors, with a block-wise scheme for distributed processing of large volumes.
ocar.resolution: On three 1.2 × 4 × 4 µm Drosophila neural-tissue volumes they report speed-ups of three orders of magnitude and a 53% accuracy increase versus prior art. They release a densely annotated CREMI-based benchmark of eight 30 × 1000 × 1000 voxel blocks (1.2 × 4 × 4 µm).
ocar.future_work: The ILP and block-wise solver are intended to scale microtubule tracking to very large EM volumes.

summaries.beginner: Inside neurons, tiny tubes called microtubules can be seen in electron-microscope pictures, but following them by computer was slow and error-prone. This method traces them much faster and more accurately and shares a labeled test set.
summaries.intermediate: At MICCAI (2020), Eckstein et al. track microtubules in EM by enumerating candidate edges among likely voxels and solving a constrained ILP with biological priors. Versus prior art on three 1.2 × 4 × 4 µm Drosophila neural volumes, they report ~1000× speed-up and 53% higher accuracy, plus a block-wise solver for large volumes. They release eight densely annotated 1.2 × 4 × 4 µm CREMI blocks as a benchmark.
summaries.advanced: The 53% accuracy increase and three-order speed-up are relative to a specified prior on those three small volumes; they may not hold at whole-brain scale. Voxel size 30 × 1000 × 1000 at 1.2 × 4 × 4 µm implies 40 nm in z and 4 nm in x/y for the benchmark blocks. ILP tractability still depends on candidate-graph sparsity.

plain_language_summary: Inside neurons, tiny tubes called microtubules can be seen in electron-microscope pictures, but following them by computer was slow and error-prone. This method traces them much faster and more accurately and shares a labeled test set.

ocar.opportunity: Volume EM for dense circuit reconstruction is split between large-field ultramicrotomy methods with limited z-resolution and isotropic FIB-SEM with restricted volume.
ocar.challenge: Combining large context with targeted isotropic ultrastructure, and finding rare events such as microglia–amyloid contacts, is inefficient with either family alone.
ocar.action: Kislinger, Gnägi, Kerschensteiner, Simons, Misgeld, and Schifferer present ATUM-FIB: serial 2–10 µm resin sections on transparent tape, mapped by light and electron microscopy, then targeted with FIB-SEM on demand.
ocar.resolution: The serial semithick sections form a tissue library of microscopic context that can be probed locally at isotropic resolution. They demonstrate identification of microglia contact sites with amyloid plaques in a mouse model of familial Alzheimer’s disease.
ocar.future_work: The hybrid is offered for rare but pathologically important ultrastructural events within larger tissue context.

summaries.beginner: One 3D electron-microscope style can survey a large area but is coarse in depth; another is sharp in all directions but only in a tiny block. This method cuts medium-thick slices as a searchable library, then uses the sharp tool only on the interesting spots.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2020 bioRxiv/iScience paper, Kislinger et al. introduce ATUM-FIB, collecting 2–10 µm resin sections on tape, mapping them with light and EM, then targeting FIB-SEM. The section set is a tissue library for on-demand isotropic ultrastructure. They show microglia–amyloid plaque contacts in a familial Alzheimer’s mouse model.
summaries.advanced: Section thickness 2–10 µm is the library scale; isotropic FIB-SEM resolution values are not given in the abstract. The Alzheimer’s demonstration is a use-case for rare-event targeting, not a quantitative pathology study. Catalog methods include SBF-SEM, FIB-SEM, ATUM+WaferMapper, and ssTEM as the compared/combined family.

plain_language_summary: One 3D electron-microscope style can survey a large area but is coarse in depth; another is sharp in all directions but only in a tiny block. This method cuts medium-thick slices as a searchable library, then uses the sharp tool only on the interesting spots.

ocar.opportunity: The connectome concept offers a comprehensive network map of nervous-system connectivity at a chosen scale, from neurons to brain areas.
ocar.challenge: Applying that concept to human structural and functional connectivity, development, and clinical differences requires a clear definition and a survey of topology-to-dynamics links.
ocar.action: Sporns provides a textbook chapter overview of origins and definitions, structural versus functional connectivity, major findings on human connectome topology, how structure shapes dynamics, and individual differences.
ocar.resolution: Connectome maps are presented as complete, systematic accounts of anatomical or physiological relationships at a given scale, with topology constraining dynamic activity.
ocar.future_work: Themes include development and clinical populations as active application areas.

summaries.beginner: A “connectome” is a full list of how parts of a nervous system are linked, at whatever zoom you choose. This textbook chapter explains the idea and what has been learned about human brain networks.
summaries.intermediate: In the New Oxford Textbook of Psychiatry (2020), Olaf Sporns overviews the connectome concept: neural elements and their interconnections as a complete map at a given scale. He surveys structural and functional human connectivity, topological findings, how structure shapes dynamics, and individual differences in development and clinical groups.
summaries.advanced: This is a textbook chapter, not original data. “Complete” is scale-relative by definition in the text. Clinical and developmental themes are a selection of current topics, not a meta-analysis. Distinguish this MRI/network-neuroscience usage of “connectome” from synapse-resolution EM connectomes elsewhere in the corpus.

plain_language_summary: A “connectome” is a full list of how parts of a nervous system are linked, at whatever zoom you choose. This textbook chapter explains the idea and what has been learned about human brain networks.

ocar.opportunity: Mipmaps of segmentation volumes store, in each coarser voxel, a mixture (histogram) of segmentation IDs from children, which is useful for rendering and queries but storage-heavy.
ocar.challenge: Compressing, rendering with transfer functions, and querying partial histograms over footprints at interactive rates is hard for large label volumes.
ocar.action: Althelaya, Agus, and Schneider introduce the Mixture Graph: mixtures are factorized into linear interpolations between exactly two IDs, stored as a pruned, compressed DAG, with transfer functions propagated from leaves.
ocar.resolution: The structure supports efficient pre-filtered rendering at interactive frame rates, partial histogram queries up to 178× faster than naive parallelized range queries, correctly pre-filtered volume lighting, and interactive exploration with multi-dimensional transfer functions.
ocar.future_work: They present the Mixture Graph as a general data structure for segmentation-histogram volumes.

summaries.beginner: When you zoom out on a labeled 3D scan, each chunk is a mix of many cell IDs. This paper stores those mixes as a compact graph so you can color, light, and query the volume quickly.
summaries.intermediate: In IEEE TVCG (2020), Althelaya, Agus, and Schneider factor segmentation-histogram mixtures into sequences of two-ID interpolations stored as a DAG (the Mixture Graph). After pruning and compression, transfer functions propagate from sources for pre-filtered rendering. They report up to 178× speed-up for partial histogram queries versus naive parallel range queries, plus applications to pre-filtered lighting and multi-dimensional transfer-function exploration.
summaries.advanced: The 178× figure is an upper bound (“up to”) against a specified naive baseline; typical speed-ups may be lower. The method assumes convex combinations of IDs in histogram mipmaps. Domain (connectomic EM versus other label volumes) is not restricted in the abstract. Interactive rates are claimed but hardware/volume size are not given here.

plain_language_summary: When you zoom out on a labeled 3D scan, each chunk is a mix of many cell IDs. This paper stores those mixes as a compact graph so you can color, light, and query the volume quickly.

ocar.opportunity: Janelia efforts are reconstructing whole-brain connectomes of larval and adult Drosophila, extending the C. elegans precedent of a complete synaptic wiring diagram.
ocar.challenge: In a whole brain it becomes hard to isolate distinct circuits: even early sensory layers are strongly interconnected, and higher brain regions are densely linked by long-range projections and multisensory convergence, plus communication beyond direct synapses.
ocar.action: Vogt reviews how forthcoming fly whole-brain connectomes can incorporate decades of circuit information, while stressing extra-synaptic communication and genetic/behavioral tools.
ocar.resolution: The complete wiring diagram shows sensory information is not processed only in separate channels and that higher brain regions are densely interconnected. Drosophila can still combine connectomics with genetics and behavior to pursue entire-brain function.
ocar.future_work: The piece frames fly connectomes as a framework for whole-brain function, including non-synaptic modulation.

summaries.beginner: Soon the fruit fly will join the worm in having a nearly complete brain wiring list. This commentary warns that the list will show messy cross-talk, not neat separate senses, and that chemistry between cells still matters.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neurogenetics (2020), Vogt discusses upcoming larval and adult Drosophila whole-brain connectomes from Janelia in light of the C. elegans precedent. Whole-brain wiring implies strong interconnectivity even in early sensory layers and dense long-range links among higher regions. She argues fly genetics and behavior still make whole-brain function tractable despite non-synaptic communication.
summaries.advanced: This is a perspective written before those whole-brain fly connectomes were fully public; treat “will soon reconstruct” as contemporaneous outlook. Catalog dataset/organism tags say C. elegans—the abstract uses C. elegans as precedent and Drosophila as the subject. Extra-synaptic communication is flagged as necessary, not mapped here.

plain_language_summary: Soon the fruit fly will join the worm in having a nearly complete brain wiring list. This commentary warns that the list will show messy cross-talk, not neat separate senses, and that chemistry between cells still matters.

ocar.opportunity: Metastudies of tract-tracing papers are used to build connectome databases of interregional connections.
ocar.challenge: Non-standardized, often unclear descriptions mean different experts may extract different connections from the same paper, potentially distorting adjacency matrices and graph analyses; this variability had not been measured.
ocar.action: Schmitt, Eipert, and colleagues have three blinded experts extract hypothalamic subregion connections from 16 tract-tracing publications and propose a workflow to detect variability at multiple processing steps.
ocar.resolution: They find inter-rater variability, and they analyze observation scores, discrepant-connection matrix visualizations, and weight variations in adjacency matrices.
ocar.future_work: Data and software are released via neuroVIISAS; the workflow is meant to make collated connectomes more reliable.

summaries.beginner: Some brain-connection databases are typed up from old tracing papers, but the papers are not written as spreadsheets. This study asks three people to read the same sixteen papers and shows they do not always record the same links.
summaries.intermediate: In Briefings in Bioinformatics (2019), Schmitt et al. quantify inter-rater and inter-observation variability in tract-tracing-based hypothalamic connectivity extracted from 16 publications. Three blinded experts disagree on connections; the authors analyze observation scores, discrepant-connection visualizations, and adjacency-weight variation. They propose a workflow for catching variability during connectome metastudies and release data/software.
summaries.advanced: The sample is 16 hypothalamic tract-tracing papers, not a field-wide error rate. The abstract does not report a numeric inter-rater kappa. Consequences for graph analyses are motivated (“could produce significant misconstructions”) rather than demonstrated on a downstream metric here.

plain_language_summary: Some brain-connection databases are typed up from old tracing papers, but the papers are not written as spreadsheets. This study asks three people to read the same sixteen papers and shows they do not always record the same links.

ocar.opportunity: C. elegans uniquely combines a detailed neural connectivity diagram, well-characterized genomics, and relatively simple quantifiable behavior, making it a candidate for systems-level integration from molecules to behavior.
ocar.challenge: Meeting that lofty goal still faces successes and open challenges, especially from a computational perspective.
ocar.action: Karbowski reviews computational and perturbation (genome and connectome) approaches to deciphering circuits for worm behavior.
ocar.resolution: The review points out both successes and challenges in integrating molecular and cellular knowledge into a global understanding of behavior.
ocar.future_work: The systems-biology program remains an active, incomplete agenda.

summaries.beginner: The worm is the only animal with a full wiring list, a mapped genome, and simple measurable actions, so it looks perfect for a complete explanation of behavior. This review surveys how far computer models and genetic or wiring perturbations have actually gotten.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Systems Biology (2019), Karbowski reviews computational work and genome/connectome perturbations aimed at C. elegans behavior. He treats the worm as the best candidate for integrating molecular and cellular knowledge into global behavioral understanding, while cataloguing challenges. Emphasis is on the computational perspective.
summaries.advanced: This is a review; specific models and challenges are not enumerated in the abstract. The uniqueness claim (“only animals with the known detailed neural connectivity diagram”) reflects the 2019 landscape. Catalog DS01 matches the subject organism.

plain_language_summary: The worm is the only animal with a full wiring list, a mapped genome, and simple measurable actions, so it looks perfect for a complete explanation of behavior. This review surveys how far computer models and genetic or wiring perturbations have actually gotten.

ocar.opportunity: Human spinal-cord connectomes are scarce compared with brain connectomes, yet spinal circuitry is central to many biomedical questions including stimulation for analgesia.
ocar.challenge: Building even a draft map requires assembling cell types, connectivity, and strengths from mixed human and animal literature plus estimates of neuron counts.
ocar.action: Arle, Iftimia, Shils, Mei, and Carlson construct a draft human spinal-cord connectome from anatomical literature, cadaveric measurements, histology, and cytoarchitecture, then simulate it with neural-circuitry software, including all ten Rexed laminae and 31 segments.
ocar.resolution: The model includes intralaminar, interlaminar, and intersegmental connections plus ascending and descending brain links, with estimated neuron counts per cell type in every lamina of all 31 segments. They note highly interconnected recurrent networks and use the model to study spinal-cord stimulation for analgesia.
ocar.future_work: Each application needs additional calibrations; future work includes simulating additional segments and expanding research uses. The draft is a starting template for specialized-behavior overlays.

summaries.beginner: Maps of the human spinal cord’s wiring are rare compared with brain maps. This team stitches together published anatomy into a working computer model of the cord and tries it on spinal stimulation for pain.
summaries.intermediate: In Neural Computation (2019), Arle et al. assemble a draft human spinal-cord connectome from literature, cadaveric measurements, histology, and cytoarchitecture, filling all ten Rexed laminae across 31 segments with estimated neuron counts. Simulations reveal highly interconnected recurrent networks. They apply the model to spinal-cord stimulation for analgesia and stress that specialized behaviors need extra calibration.
summaries.advanced: This is a literature-derived draft, not an EM reconstruction; where human data were missing, other species were used. Neuron counts are estimates from mixed sources. “Several orders of recurrence” is qualitative. Analgesia results are not quantified in the abstract. Future work explicitly includes more segments and calibrations—treat current outputs as hypothesis-generating.

plain_language_summary: Maps of the human spinal cord’s wiring are rare compared with brain maps. This team stitches together published anatomy into a working computer model of the cord and tries it on spinal stimulation for pain.

ocar.opportunity: Volumetric correlative light and electron microscopy needs reliable, non-destructive collection of ultrathin sections onto silicon wafers for post-embedding staining.
ocar.challenge: Traditional collection demands exquisite manual skill and is tedious and unreliable, especially for hundreds of sections.
ocar.action: Templier introduces MagC: sample blocks are augmented with magnetic resin so sections can be remotely actuated and collected on wafer.
ocar.resolution: MagC enabled collection of hundreds of sections and correlative visualization of neuroanatomical tracers within their ultrastructural volumetric EM context.
ocar.future_work: The method is offered to make wafer-based CLEM collection more routine.

summaries.beginner: Stacking thousands of extremely thin slices onto a wafer for combined light and electron imaging usually takes a very steady human hand. This method mixes magnetic material into the plastic so magnets can gather the slices instead.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2019 bioRxiv paper (eLife DOI), Templier presents MagC, adding magnetic resin to blocks so ultrathin sections can be remotely collected on wafers. The approach collected hundreds of sections and allowed correlative visualization of neuroanatomical tracers in volumetric EM context. It targets a bottleneck in post-embedding CLEM.
summaries.advanced: “Hundreds of sections” is the scale claim; error rates, wrinkles, and lost-section frequency are not given. Catalog journal is bioRxiv despite an eLife DOI. Tracer visualization is the demonstrated CLEM payoff, not a circuit-discovery result.

plain_language_summary: Stacking thousands of extremely thin slices onto a wafer for combined light and electron imaging usually takes a very steady human hand. This method mixes magnetic material into the plastic so magnets can gather the slices instead.

ocar.opportunity: EM is powerful for circuit mapping, but identifying specific cell types in EM volumes remains a major challenge, especially for multiple populations at once.
ocar.challenge: Spectral separation used in light microscopy does not apply to conventional EM, so multiplexed genetic labels need orthogonal subcellular peroxidase targeting.
ocar.action: Zhang, Lee, Paul, and Ginty present 15 AAV constructs and 6 mouse reporter lines featuring dAPEX2, an improved ascorbate peroxidase targeted to different compartments, in a protocol compatible with existing EM pipelines.
ocar.resolution: Multiple orthogonal reporters can be distinguished simultaneously under EM. Proof-of-principle double and triple labeling showed synaptic connections among primary afferents, descending cortical inputs, and inhibitory interneurons in spinal dorsal horn.
ocar.future_work: They argue multiplexed peroxidase labeling should greatly facilitate connectivity analysis among genetically defined populations.

summaries.beginner: Electron-microscope pictures rarely tell you which genetic cell type you are looking at, and you usually cannot color several types at once. This paper creates stronger chemical labels parked in different parts of the cell so several types can be seen together in the same electron-microscope volume.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Neuroscience (2019), Zhang et al. introduce multiplexed EM labeling with dAPEX2, which has dramatically improved signal over prior ascorbate peroxidases. Fifteen AAV constructs and six mouse reporter lines target the enzyme to different subcellular compartments so orthogonal reporters are distinguishable without spectral separation, in pipelines compatible with existing EM. Double and triple labeling in spinal dorsal horn revealed synapses among primary afferents, corticospinal inputs, and inhibitory interneurons.
summaries.advanced: “Dramatically improved signal” is qualitative. The spinal-cord experiment is proof-of-principle for double/triple labeling, not a full dorsal-horn connectome. Compatibility with existing EM pipelines is asserted; stain/osmium interactions should still be checked per protocol. Catalog organism is mouse, matching the reporter lines.

plain_language_summary: Electron-microscope pictures rarely tell you which genetic cell type you are looking at, and you usually cannot color several types at once. This paper creates stronger chemical labels parked in different parts of the cell so several types can be seen together in the same electron-microscope volume.

ocar.opportunity: The 1986 C. elegans connectome was a milestone for relating wiring to behavior; subsequent technologies now link neural activity patterns to behavior and sensory modulation.
ocar.challenge: Understanding how the connectome’s developmental origins, cell lineages, and biophysical dynamics produce behavior requires integrating experiment with whole-organism models.
ocar.action: DiLoreto, Chute, Bryce, and Srinivasan review technological advances in functional connectomics: activity–behavior links, developmental origins, computational modeling of single-neuron biophysics and whole-organism networks, and tools to perturb neuronal function.
ocar.resolution: Combining experimental datasets with theoretical modeling is presented as the path to better understanding organismal behavior, interrogating local and global circuits.
ocar.future_work: They argue combining these approaches will show how networks process sensory information into appropriate behavioral output, toward a complete understanding of the worm nervous system.

summaries.beginner: The first full animal wiring diagram came from a worm in the 1980s. This review covers newer tools that watch, model, and perturb that wiring while the animal behaves.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Developmental Biology (2019), DiLoreto et al. review functional-connectomics advances in C. elegans since the 1986 structure/connectivity milestone. Themes include linking activity to behavior, developmental origins and cell lineage, computational models from single-neuron biophysics to whole-organism networks, and perturbation technologies. The goal is integrating experiment and theory for sensory-to-behavior processing.
summaries.advanced: This is a review of tools and concepts, not a new connectome. “Complete understanding” is an aspirational closing line. Catalog DS01 matches the organism.

plain_language_summary: The first full animal wiring diagram came from a worm in the 1980s. This review covers newer tools that watch, model, and perturb that wiring while the animal behaves.

ocar.opportunity: Axonal morphology is an essential cell-type descriptor and shows how neurons route output across the brain, but few mouse projection neurons have been reconstructed in their entirety.
ocar.challenge: Imaging and reconstructing complete axonal arbors that span substantial portions of the brain has been inefficient.
ocar.action: Winnubst, Bas, Ferreira, Svoboda, Chandrashekar, and colleagues present a platform for complete neuronal morphologies and reconstruct more than 1,000 projection neurons in motor cortex, thalamus, subiculum, and hypothalamus.
ocar.resolution: Together the neurons comprise more than 75 meters of axonal length and are available in a searchable online database. Axonal shapes revealed previously unknown projection-neuron subtypes and suggest organizational principles of long-range connectivity.
ocar.future_work: The database is offered as a resource for cell-type and long-range-connectivity research.

summaries.beginner: A brain cell’s long-distance cable, the axon, often wanders through much of the brain, but few mouse cells have been drawn in full. This project traces more than a thousand of them and puts the drawings in a searchable collection.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2019 bioRxiv preprint, Winnubst et al. describe a platform for imaging and reconstructing complete mouse projection-neuron morphologies, including long-range axons. They reconstruct more than 1,000 neurons in motor cortex, thalamus, subiculum, and hypothalamus, totaling more than 75 meters of axon, released in a searchable database. Axonal shapes reveal previously unknown subtypes and suggest organizing principles of long-range connectivity.
summaries.advanced: This is mesoscale full-morphology reconstruction, not synapse-resolution EM connectomics. “Previously unknown subtypes” are not listed in the abstract. 1,000+ neurons and 75+ meters are the scale claims; completeness still depends on labeling and tracing criteria in the full paper. Catalog journal is bioRxiv (MouseLight resource era).

plain_language_summary: A brain cell’s long-distance cable, the axon, often wanders through much of the brain, but few mouse cells have been drawn in full. This project traces more than a thousand of them and puts the drawings in a searchable collection.

ocar.opportunity: Spectral analysis of structural connectomes can reveal organizational peculiarities not obvious from standard graph metrics, including possible signatures of criticality.
ocar.challenge: Whether human connectomes are spectrally distinctive relative to other organisms, and whether their graph-Laplacian spacing matches a critical regime, was untested in this comparative way.
ocar.action: Pospelov, Nechaev, Anokhin, Valba, Avetisov, and Gorsky perform comparative spectral analysis of structural connectomes from open-access data, including human versus other organisms, network-evolution models with 3-cycle preference, and human graph-Laplacian level spacing.
ocar.resolution: Human spectral density shows the maximal deviation from a randomized network among organisms studied. Many non-human connectomes are well reproduced by evolution preferring 3-cycles, but human fits require conserving local clustering. Human Laplacian spacing matches the critical hybrid of Wigner–Dyson and Poisson statistics, supporting a brain-criticality claim.
ocar.future_work: They present the critical spectral statistics as strong support for the debated brain-criticality hypothesis.

summaries.beginner: If you look at a brain network like a vibrating shape, its “tones” can reveal hidden organization. This study says the human wiring diagram’s tones stand out from other animals and look like a system poised at a special balance point.
summaries.intermediate: In Physics of Life Reviews (2019), Pospelov et al. compare structural-connectome spectra across organisms using open-access data. The human connectome’s spectral density deviates most from a randomized null. Preference for 3-cycle formation reproduces many animal connectomes, but human evolution in their model requires conserving local clustering. Graph-Laplacian level spacing matches a critical Wigner–Dyson/Poisson hybrid familiar in condensed-matter physics.
summaries.advanced: “Maximal deviation” is among the organisms in their open-access set, not a proof of uniqueness among all animals. Structural connectomes here are likely MRI-scale, not EM. Criticality is inferred from spectral statistics, a debated mapping. 3-cycle evolutionary models are phenomenological fits. Human local-clustering conservation is required for their fit, not independently measured as a developmental mechanism.

plain_language_summary: If you look at a brain network like a vibrating shape, its “tones” can reveal hidden organization. This study says the human wiring diagram’s tones stand out from other animals and look like a system poised at a special balance point.

ocar.opportunity: Deep networks are considered vital for expanding biomedical image datasets, including EM, X-ray, and light microscopy.
ocar.challenge: Community access is limited by complex computational environments and scarce high-performance hardware.
ocar.action: Haberl, Churas, Ellisman, and colleagues present CDeep3M, a cloud-based, ready-to-use deep convolutional network for image segmentation, and benchmark it on large 2D and 3D light, X-ray, and electron-microscopy datasets.
ocar.resolution: CDeep3M provides a user-friendly cloud tool for deep-learning segmentation, demonstrated on challenging multi-modal microscopy tasks.
ocar.future_work: Cloud delivery is intended to remove local HPC and environment-setup bottlenecks.

summaries.beginner: Computers can outline cells in microscope pictures, but setting up the software and big computers is a barrier. This paper puts a ready-made outlining tool in the cloud so more labs can use it.
summaries.intermediate: In Nature Methods (2018), Haberl et al. introduce CDeep3M, a plug-and-play cloud deep CNN for biomedical image segmentation. They benchmark large, complex 2D and 3D datasets from light, X-ray, and electron microscopy. The tool is framed as lowering barriers from environment setup and HPC access.
summaries.advanced: Benchmarks are described as demonstrations on challenging tasks; numeric scores are not in the abstract. Cloud dependence trades local HPC for service availability and data-upload constraints. “Plug-and-play” still requires annotations for training/finetuning in typical CNN workflows, not detailed here.

plain_language_summary: Computers can outline cells in microscope pictures, but setting up the software and big computers is a barrier. This paper puts a ready-made outlining tool in the cloud so more labs can use it.

ocar.opportunity: Automated segmentation has become necessary for volume EM, with fully supervised encoder–decoders performing best when abundant annotations exist.
ocar.challenge: Domain shifts (e.g., brain versus HeLa cells, isotropic FIB/SEM versus anisotropic TEM) force costly new annotation; classification-oriented domain adaptation is underexplored for volume EM segmentation.
ocar.action: Roels, Hennies, Saeys, Philips, and Kreshuk extend classification DA methods to encoder–decoders and propose adding a reconstruction decoder to align source and target encoder features, validated on mitochondria segmentation.
ocar.resolution: The method outperforms extended classification DA techniques and a finetuning baseline for brain→HeLa and FIB/SEM→TEM mitochondria tasks.
ocar.future_work: Code is released to support further domain-adaptive EM segmentation.

summaries.beginner: A cell-outlining program trained on one kind of electron-microscope sample often fails on another. This paper adapts the program using fewer new labels by making it also reconstruct the pictures, and tests it on mitochondria.
summaries.intermediate: At ISBI (2018/2019), Roels et al. extend domain-adaptation ideas from classification to encoder–decoder segmentation and add a reconstruction decoder to align source and target encoder features. On mitochondria in volume EM, they adapt from brain images to HeLa cells and from isotropic FIB/SEM to anisotropic TEM. The proposed method outperforms extended classification DA methods and finetuning.
summaries.advanced: Only mitochondria segmentation is validated, not membranes or synapses. Outperformance is stated without numeric scores in the abstract. Reconstruction-decoder alignment is the novel ingredient versus “extended classification DA.” Code link is provided for inspection of training protocols.

plain_language_summary: A cell-outlining program trained on one kind of electron-microscope sample often fails on another. This paper adapts the program using fewer new labels by making it also reconstruct the pictures, and tests it on mitochondria.

ocar.opportunity: The tadpole larva of Ciona intestinalis, a chordate sibling, has a sparsely populated nervous system now documented at EM connectome level for both central and peripheral systems.
ocar.challenge: Translating those reconstructions into a coherent account of neuron types, chordate versus idiosyncratic features, and synaptic style required a synthesis of sporadic earlier studies plus two recent connectome reports.
ocar.action: Ryan and Meinertzhagen review Ciona larval neuron types in light of those EM connectomes.
ocar.resolution: About 330 CNS cells are mostly ciliated ependymal cells, with roughly 180 neurons in about 50 morphologically distinguishable types. Most neurons are ciliated and lack dendrites; some lack axons. Synapses are mostly en passant, often dyads, with heterogeneous vesicles; each neuron averages 49 synapses, forming a network of unpredicted complexity.
ocar.future_work: The inventory is a baseline for relating this simple chordate circuit to vertebrate neuronal identity.

summaries.beginner: A sea-squirt tadpole is a simple cousin of backboned animals and now has a full list of its nerve cells and contacts. This review counts those cell types and notes that many cells lack the textbook dendrites and axons.
summaries.intermediate: In Current Opinion in Neurobiology (2018), Ryan and Meinertzhagen synthesize Ciona intestinalis larval neuron types from EM connectomes of central and peripheral nervous systems. About 330 CNS cells include mostly ciliated ependymal cells and ~180 neurons in ~50 morphological types. Neurons are typically ciliated, often without dendrites and sometimes without axons; synapses are mostly en passant (some dyads) with mixed vesicles, averaging 49 synapses per neuron.
summaries.advanced: Counts (~330, ~180, ~50, average 49) come from the reviewed reconstructions; “unpredicted complexity” is qualitative. Synapses resembling basal invertebrates is a comparative remark. Catalog dataset DS20 Ciona matches the organism. This is a review, not a new volume.

plain_language_summary: A sea-squirt tadpole is a simple cousin of backboned animals and now has a full list of its nerve cells and contacts. This review counts those cell types and notes that many cells lack the textbook dendrites and axons.

ocar.opportunity: Connectome mapping often assumes connections are stable once formed, yet rewiring could change communication pathways in healthy adult brains and in disease.
ocar.challenge: Evidence for rewiring has been difficult to obtain, and it is unclear at which scales—from synapses to long-range tracts—adult circuitry can reorganize, especially during learning.
ocar.action: Bennett, Kirby, and Finnerty review evidence for rewiring at multiple connectome scales and consider its role in learning and therapy.
ocar.resolution: New evidence indicates local circuitry is rewired during learning. The connectome is more dynamic than a static map implies. Harnessing rewiring is proposed as offering new treatment avenues for psychiatric and neurological disease.
ocar.future_work: They conclude that exploiting rewiring could yield new therapeutic strategies.

summaries.beginner: Brain-wiring maps are often drawn as if the cables stay put. This review gathers evidence that local circuits can be re-plugged during learning, and that doctors might one day use that flexibility as treatment.
summaries.intermediate: In Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews (2018), Bennett, Kirby, and Finnerty examine rewiring across connectome scales from synapses and microcircuits to long-range tracts. They argue evidence has been hard to get, but new data indicate local circuitry rewires during learning, so adult mammalian connectomes are more dynamic than often assumed. Harnessing rewiring is discussed as a therapeutic direction.
summaries.advanced: This is a review; “new evidence” is not itemized in the abstract. Therapeutic claims are prospective. Distinguish synaptic weight change from true anatomical rewiring when reading the full text. Scale-specific evidence quality likely differs from microcircuit to tractography.

plain_language_summary: Brain-wiring maps are often drawn as if the cables stay put. This review gathers evidence that local circuits can be re-plugged during learning, and that doctors might one day use that flexibility as treatment.

ocar.opportunity: Fine-scale synaptic organization of hippocampal CA1 neurons innervated by Schaffer collaterals is an important determinant of circuit function.
ocar.challenge: Whether excitatory pyramidal cells and inhibitory parvalbumin interneurons follow the same spatial connectivity rules, and how Peters’ rule and deep versus superficial CA1 sublayers affect those patterns, was unknown.
ocar.action: Kwon, Feng, Druckmann, and Kim analyze CA3→CA1 connectivity with mGRASP in male mice, comparing pyramidal cells and PV interneurons.
ocar.resolution: Pyramidal cells show spatially structured synaptic connectivity, enhanced when Peters’ rule is applied for prediction, and deep-sublayer pyramids appear more structured than superficial ones. PV cells are significantly more random, become more random under Peters’ rule, and show little sublayer specificity.
ocar.future_work: Different excitatory versus inhibitory fine-scale structure is offered as insight for hippocampal network development and theory.

summaries.beginner: In the hippocampus, incoming cables from one area land on both activating and calming cells. This mouse study finds the activating cells follow a spatial wiring pattern, while a class of calming cells looks much more random.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Neuroscience (2018), Kwon et al. use mGRASP to map Schaffer-collateral synapses onto CA1 pyramids and PV interneurons in male mice. CA3–CA1 pyramidal connectivity is spatially structured (more so in deep than superficial stratum pyramidale) and becomes more structured when Peters’ rule is used for synapse prediction. PV connectivity is more random, is made more random by Peters’ rule, and lacks clear sublayer specificity.
summaries.advanced: Results are from male mice and mGRASP-detected contacts; physiological synapse strength is not the readout. Peters’ rule here is used as a prediction overlay, not as a claim that overlap equals connectivity. “Significantly more random” lacks a statistic in the abstract. Structured vs random is about spatial organization of contacts, not absence of specificity in other features.

plain_language_summary: In the hippocampus, incoming cables from one area land on both activating and calming cells. This mouse study finds the activating cells follow a spatial wiring pattern, while a class of calming cells looks much more random.

ocar.opportunity: Large-scale connectome projects are underway across species, but the first complete animal connectome—White et al., 1986, reconstructing 302 C. elegans neurons from serial EM—still anchors the field.
ocar.challenge: Remembering what that manual reconstruction actually delivered, and how it continues to guide neurobiology and network science, is easy to lose amid newer volumes.
ocar.action: Schafer reviews the worm connectome’s origins, content (morphology plus chemical and electrical synapses), and lasting influence.
ocar.resolution: The wiring diagram profoundly influenced behavioral neurobiology and network science and still offers a guide for how connectomics can impact neurobiology.
ocar.future_work: The essay is framed as “back to the future”: using the classic worm map as a standard for what complete connectomes should enable.

summaries.beginner: The first complete animal wiring diagram was drawn by hand from worm electron-microscope pictures in 1986. This short piece explains why that map still matters as bigger brains are mapped today.
summaries.intermediate: In Trends in Neurosciences (2018), Schafer revisits White et al. 1986: serial-EM reconstruction of all 302 adult C. elegans neurons and their chemical and electrical synapses. He reviews how that first complete connectome shaped behavioral neurobiology and network science. The essay uses the worm as a guide for the impact expected from modern connectomics.
summaries.advanced: This is a historical perspective, not a re-reconstruction. “302 neurons” is the canonical adult hermaphrodite count as stated. Influence claims are scholarly, not bibliometric, in the abstract. Catalog DS01 and EM tags match the subject.

plain_language_summary: The first complete animal wiring diagram was drawn by hand from worm electron-microscope pictures in 1986. This short piece explains why that map still matters as bigger brains are mapped today.

ocar.opportunity: Spinal interneurons coordinate motoneurons for locomotion, but it is controversial whether orderly motoneuron recruitment is mostly due to motoneuron biophysics or to specific interneuron wiring onto motoneuron subsets.
ocar.challenge: Average connectivity cannot settle whether speed-related interneurons specifically target large, high-force motoneurons.
ocar.action: Svara, Kornfeld, Denk, and Bollmann map all connections from two interneuron types onto all motoneurons in a larval zebrafish spinal hemisegment using serial block-face EM.
ocar.resolution: Dorsal, but not ventral, excitatory ipsilateral interneurons show specific connectivity: large motoneurons active only when strong force is required receive specific input from dorsal interneurons active only during fast swims. Inhibitory commissural–motoneuron connectivity lacks a discernible pattern. Wiring is consistent with recruitment that depends considerably on specific connectivity.
ocar.future_work: The complete local map is a structural answer to the recruitment debate for this circuit.

summaries.beginner: When a fish swims faster, bigger muscle-driving cells join in—but is that because those cells are built differently, or because they get special incoming wires? A complete 3D electron-microscope map of one spinal segment finds special wires onto the big cells from cells that fire only in fast swims.
summaries.intermediate: In Cell Reports (2018), Svara et al. reconstruct all synapses from two interneuron types onto all motoneurons in a larval zebrafish spinal hemisegment with SBEM. Dorsal excitatory ipsilateral interneurons specifically innervate large, high-force motoneurons; ventral ones do not. Inhibitory commissural connections to motoneurons lack a clear pattern. The authors conclude recruitment depends to a considerable extent on specific connectivity, not only biophysics.
summaries.advanced: The map is one hemisegment; “all connections from two types onto all motoneurons” is local completeness, not whole-cord completeness. Functional labels (fast swims, high force) are tied to known physiology of those cell classes as used in the paper’s framing. “No discernible pattern” for inhibitory commissurals is a negative anatomical result. Catalog DS15 zebrafish and SBF-SEM match.

plain_language_summary: When a fish swims faster, bigger muscle-driving cells join in—but is that because those cells are built differently, or because they get special incoming wires? A complete 3D electron-microscope map of one spinal segment finds special wires onto the big cells from cells that fire only in fast swims.

ocar.opportunity: Understanding wiring specificity requires both synaptic connectivity and the spatial proximity of neurons, which volumetric reconstructions can supply.
ocar.challenge: How much of C. elegans nerve-ring synaptic specificity is explained by process placement versus additional non-spatial factors was unquantified, including changes between larval and adult stages.
ocar.action: Brittin, Cook, Hall, Emmons, and Cohen volumetrically reconstruct the C. elegans nerve ring from legacy serial-section EM at L4 and young adult, then analyze neighborhoods, synapse types, and placement versus connectivity.
ocar.resolution: They describe three levels of specificity—spatial, synaptic, and subcellular. Process-placement variability accounts for less than 20% of synaptic-connectivity variability; spatial models cannot account for homologous-neuron connection reproducibility. They conjecture a spatially constrained genetic model, showing that extra specificity such as subcellular domains or alternative splicing would be required.
ocar.future_work: The volumetric maps are a resource for models that combine geometry with cell-specific gene expression.

summaries.beginner: In a worm’s central nerve bundle, cells that sit near each other still do not all connect. By rebuilding that bundle in 3D at two ages, this team shows that location explains only a small part of who synapses with whom.
summaries.intermediate: In a 2018 preprint, Brittin et al. volumetrically reconstruct the C. elegans nerve ring from legacy serial EM at L4 and young adult. They report spatial, synaptic, and subcellular specificity: classes innervate defined neighborhoods and aggregate functionally similar synapses. Placement variability explains less than 20% of connectivity variability, so non-spatial factors are needed; even a combinatorial genetic model would require extra devices such as subcellular domains or splicing.
summaries.advanced: “Less than 20%” is the stated fraction of connectivity variability explained by process placement. Legacy EM limits resolution/completeness relative to modern volumes. The genetic-expression model is a conjecture demonstrating insufficiency of simple combinatorial codes, not a measured splicing map. Empty journal field in the catalog; treat as bioRxiv 10.1101/485771.

plain_language_summary: In a worm’s central nerve bundle, cells that sit near each other still do not all connect. By rebuilding that bundle in 3D at two ages, this team shows that location explains only a small part of who synapses with whom.

ocar.opportunity: The cone photoreceptor synapse has canonical motifs (ON invaginating versus OFF basal contacts; bipolar cells sampling all cones in their dendritic span) that shape signal transfer to bipolar and horizontal cells.
ocar.challenge: EM and immunolabeling established those motifs but traded sample size against resolution, limiting quantitative population analysis, and a published mouse volume lacked synaptic labels.
ocar.action: Rogerson, Behrens, Euler, Berens, and Schubert exploit characteristic anatomical motifs to identify putative synaptic contacts in a 3D serial-EM mouse dataset and quantitatively describe outer-retinal connectivity.
ocar.resolution: They find exceptions to classical motifs, including substantial rod–cone pathway interaction at the photoreceptor synapse, sparse photoreceptor sampling, and atypical contacts.
ocar.future_work: They discuss implications, limitations of unlabeled putative synapses, and avenues for future labeled reconstructions.

summaries.beginner: In the outer retina, textbooks say certain cell types always touch photoreceptors in set ways. Re-examining a 3D mouse map, this team finds extra mixing between rod and cone pathways and cells that skip some of their expected partners.
summaries.intermediate: In Journal of Physiology (2017), Rogerson et al. derive a quantitative outer-retina connectivity description from 3D serial EM, inferring putative synapses from canonical anatomical motifs because the published mouse volume lacks synaptic labels. They report exceptions including substantial rod–cone interaction at the photoreceptor synapse, sparse sampling, and atypical contacts. The article also reviews classic ON/OFF motifs and sampling rules.
summaries.advanced: Putative contacts inferred from morphology without synaptic labels are a central caveat the authors themselves emphasize. “Substantial” rod–cone interaction is qualitative in the abstract. Results depend on motif-based synapse calling and may miss noncanonical synapses. Catalog DS09/DS10 mouse retina and EM match the dataset class.

plain_language_summary: In the outer retina, textbooks say certain cell types always touch photoreceptors in set ways. Re-examining a 3D mouse map, this team finds extra mixing between rod and cone pathways and cells that skip some of their expected partners.

ocar.opportunity: Template matching by normalized cross correlation is widely used to find image correspondences, including assembling serial-section EM into 3D stacks for connectomics.
ocar.challenge: NCC is not robust enough when emerging petascale datasets may require billions of template matches; false matches must be driven near zero.
ocar.action: Buniatyan, Macrina, Ih, Zung, and Seung preprocess images with siamese convolutional networks trained to maximize contrast between NCC values of true versus false matches, quantified on serial-section EM brain patches.
ocar.resolution: Relative to a parameter-tuned bandpass filter, siamese nets significantly reduce false matches, and remaining false matches can be eliminated by discarding a tiny fraction of matches based on NCC values.
ocar.future_work: They expect the method to generalize to other computer-vision applications that use NCC correspondences.
